title: Salaries
outcomes: Explain the basis of charge and the meaning of salary, perquisites and profits in lieu of salary.
Determine exempt and taxable allowances under both regimes, including HRA and LTC.
Value accommodation, car and other perquisites; identify specified employees.
Apply provisions on provident funds, NPS and employer contributions.
Compute deductions for retirement benefits and income under "Salaries" in both regimes.

meta.exam_tip: A full salary computation under both regimes is almost certain; know HRA, RFA, car, gratuity, commuted pension, leave encashment limits and the ₹75,000/₹50,000 standard deduction.

concepts.title: When salary is taxed (s. 15) and employer–employee relation
body: Under section 15, salary is caught in the year it falls due or the year it is paid, if that comes first. Advance salary is taxed when received and not again when due; arrears taxed on due basis are not taxed again on receipt. Arrears that were never due earlier (e.g. retrospective pay revision) are taxed on receipt. Relief u/s 157 spreads the extra tax burden of arrears or advance salary over the years concerned.
A loan or advance against salary is not salary. Employer includes a former employer.

An employer–employee relationship is essential: an artist employed by a film company earns salary from it, but fees from producers directly are professional income. A director's commission is salary only if he is an employee. A partner's salary from his firm is business income. MPs' and MLAs' remuneration is income from other sources.

Part-time or multiple employments are all salary. Salary waived after accrual is still taxable (application of income); salary surrendered to the Government under the Voluntary Surrender of Salaries Act is exempt. Tax paid by the employer on salary is added to salary, but tax paid by the employer on non-monetary perquisites is exempt (Schedule III, Table Sl. No. 10).

Non-citizens: embassy officials (reciprocity), employees of foreign enterprises not doing business in India staying ≤ 90 days, non-resident foreign-ship crew staying ≤ 90 days, and foreign-government trainees are exempt under Schedule IV — in both regimes.
concepts.analogy: Salary is caught at the earlier of two gates — when it is due or when it is paid — but only once.
concepts.work: March salary paid on 2 April 2027 is income of tax year 2026-27.

concepts.title: Salary, perquisites and profits in lieu (ss. 16–18)
body: Salary (s. 16) includes wages, annuity or pension, gratuity, fees, commission, perquisites, profits in lieu of salary, advance salary, leave encashment, taxable portion of provident fund accretions and transfers, and contributions by the Central Government or any employer to the employee's pension account under s. 124.

Perquisites (s. 17) are benefits in cash or kind in addition to salary — accommodation, car, services, free education, concessional loans, gifts, employer contributions to PF/NPS/superannuation above ₹7.5 lakh, etc. Reimbursement of official expenses is not a perquisite.

Profits in lieu of salary (s. 18) include compensation on termination or modification of employment terms, payments from unrecognised funds (employer's share), keyman insurance sums received, and amounts received before joining or after leaving employment.
Fees and commission (fixed or as % of turnover/profits) are fully taxable.
concepts.analogy: Salary is the cash; perquisites are the perks; profits in lieu are the "goodbye" or "hello" cheques.
concepts.work: A joining bonus paid before the employee starts work is profit in lieu of salary.

concepts.title: Allowances and their exemptions
body: Allowances are fixed cash amounts. Their treatment is summarised in the table. Under the default regime only the travel/transfer/daily/conveyance allowances (to the extent spent) and transport allowance for disabled employees are exempt; others become fully taxable.

HRA (Rule 279) is exempt only in the optional regime and only if the employee pays rent for a house he does not own. "Salary" for HRA = basic + DA forming part of retirement benefits + turnover-based commission, for the period of occupation.

LTC (Schedule III, Table Sl. No. 8; Rule 278) covers travel within India on leave or after retirement for the employee and family (spouse, children; dependent parents, brothers, sisters), limited to actual expense and to air economy-class entitlement, first-class AC rail, deluxe bus, or ₹30/km where no public transport exists; two journeys in a block of four calendar years with one carry-forward; children limit of two born after 30 September 1998 (multiple births after the first child excepted).
concepts.analogy: Allowances are labelled envelopes — some envelopes are tax-free only if spent on what the label says.
concepts.work: Salaried people often shift to the optional regime mainly to use HRA and LTC exemptions.

concepts.title: Valuing perquisites: accommodation and car
body: Accommodation (table): value depends on who provides it and city population (2011 census) for employer-owned houses; leased houses take the lower of lease rent and 10% of salary. Furniture adds 10% p.a. of cost. "Salary" here includes all monetary payments (basic, DA forming part of retirement benefits, bonus, commission, taxable allowances) but excludes perquisites, exempt allowances, employer's PF contribution and lump-sum terminal benefits.
Judges of the High Court and Supreme Court: rent-free official residence and LTC are tax-free (if they opt out of the default regime).

Motor car (table): taxable only for specified employees, except where the employee's own car is used wholly for personal purposes and the employer reimburses running costs — then taxable for all employees.
concepts.analogy: Housing perquisites are a percentage of salary because the value of a company flat grows with seniority.
concepts.work: A manager living in a company-owned flat in Mumbai is taxed on 10% of salary less any rent he pays.

concepts.title: Other perquisites and specified employees
body: Specified employee: a director, a person holding 20% or more of voting power, or one whose monetary salary exceeds ₹4 lakh. For them only: car (normal cases), sweeper/gardener/watchman/attendant (employer's cost − recovery), gas, electricity and water (amount paid to supplier or manufacturing cost if self-produced − recovery), free or concessional education for household members (cost, or cost in a similar nearby institution where employer-run — no perquisite up to ₹3,000 p.m. per child).

For all employees: interest-free or concessional loans above ₹2 lakh (SBI rate on 1st day of the tax year on maximum monthly balance − interest paid); free food beyond ₹200 per meal during office hours or via paid vouchers; gifts or vouchers of ₹15,000 or more (whole value); use of movable assets; transfer of movable assets (cost − wear and tear − recovery); life insurance or annuity premium paid by employer; obligations of the employee paid by the employer (e.g. professional tax).
Tax-free for all: training and refresher-course expenses, and the specified medical facilities as per the rules.
concepts.analogy: Some perks are taxed only for the bosses (specified employees); others — loans, gifts, food — for everyone.
concepts.work: A ₹14,000 Diwali gift voucher is tax-free; a ₹16,000 one is fully taxable.

concepts.title: Provident funds, NPS and employer contributions
body: Kinds of provident fund: recognised (RPF, including EPF), unrecognised (URPF), statutory (SPF) and public (PPF).

Employer's aggregate contribution to RPF, NPS (s. 124(1)) and approved superannuation funds exceeding ₹7.5 lakh in a tax year is a taxable perquisite (s. 17(1)(h)), along with income accrued on that excess.

Interest credited to RPF above 9.5% p.a. is taxable as salary. Interest on an employee's own contribution above ₹2.5 lakh a year (₹5 lakh where the employer does not contribute), made on or after 1 April 2021, is taxable (Rule 277, separate taxable account).

Withdrawal from RPF is exempt if 5 years' continuous service, or earlier exit due to ill-health, closure or reasons beyond control, or transfer to a new employer's RPF or to NPS. From URPF: employer's share and interest are salary; interest on own contribution is other sources; own contribution not taxable.

Employer contributions to NPS are included in salary but deductible u/s 124(1)/(2) up to 14% of salary (Government, and any employer under the default regime) or 10% (other employers, optional regime) — in both regimes. Employee's own contribution deductions (ss. 123, 124(3)/(4)) need the optional regime.
concepts.analogy: Retirement funds are tax-friendly up to a point — the law caps very large employer contributions and very large employee savings.
concepts.work: A CEO whose employer puts ₹8 lakh into NPS pays tax on ₹50,000 as a perquisite beyond the ₹7.5 lakh cap.

concepts.title: Retirement benefits: gratuity, pension, leave salary, VRS
body: Under the 2025 Act, retirement benefits are included in gross salary and relief is given as deductions u/s 19(1) (table).

Gratuity received during service is fully taxable. "Salary" for gratuity: basic + DA (covered employees); basic + DA forming part of retirement benefits + turnover-based commission (not covered; average of 10 months before the retirement month). Gratuity received by widow, children or dependants on death is exempt to the same extent (Schedule III, Table Sl. No. 38).

Pension: uncommuted pension is fully taxable; commuted pension is deductible fully for Government-type employees, and for others up to one-third (if gratuity received) or one-half (if not) of the full commuted value. Gallantry-award pensions and family pensions, and disability pensions of invalided armed-forces personnel, are exempt.
Leave encashment during service is fully taxable; on retirement, fully deductible for Government employees and limited for others.
Retrenchment and voluntary retirement compensation have separate ₹5 lakh-capped deductions.
concepts.analogy: Retirement benefits enter gross salary first and then leave through the deduction door — fully for Government employees, partly for others.
concepts.work: A private employee with ₹24 lakh gratuity can deduct at most ₹20 lakh.

blocks.title: Deductions from gross salary

concepts.title: Deductions u/s 19 and computing income under both regimes
body: Gross salary less deductions u/s 19(1) gives income under "Salaries": standard deduction ₹75,000 (default) or ₹50,000 (optional); professional tax (optional regime only); and the retirement-benefit deductions (both regimes).

Proforma: basic, fees, commission, bonus, allowances (net of exemptions), taxable PF interest and employer NPS contribution, perquisites, LTC (net), gratuity, pension, retrenchment and VRS compensation, leave encashment → gross salary → deductions → net.

To move from the default to the optional regime figure: add back the extra ₹25,000 standard deduction, then subtract professional tax, HRA, education/hostel allowance, helper/research/uniform, field-area allowances and LTC exemptions.
concepts.analogy: The same pay slip gives two different salary incomes depending on which regime's lens you use.
concepts.work: Payroll software computes TDS under the default regime unless the employee declares the optional regime.

jobs.title: Year-end salary TDS check
jobs.situation: An employee asks whether to declare the optional regime to the employer.
steps: Compute salary under both regimes (HRA, LTC, professional tax, standard deduction).
Add other income and Chapter VIII deductions available only in the optional regime.
Compare tax and advise; remind that salaried employees can switch while filing the return.
jobs.takeaway: Regime choice is a computation, not a guess.

jobs.title: Retirement settlement
jobs.situation: A private-sector employee receives gratuity, leave encashment and commutes one-third of pension.
steps: Apply 19(1) deductions: gratuity (Gratuity Act formula, ₹20 lakh), leave (₹25 lakh limit), commuted pension (⅓ of full value as gratuity received).
Note uncommuted pension remains fully taxable.
jobs.takeaway: Each terminal benefit has its own limit — compute them separately.

mcqs.q: Salary is chargeable to tax on:
options: Due or receipt basis, whichever is earlier
mcqs.explain: Section 15 taxes salary in the year it becomes due or is paid, if payment comes first, and never twice. Advance salary is taxed on receipt; March salary paid in April is taxed on due basis. In practice: payroll years follow the tax year.
mcqs.topic: When salary is taxed (s. 15) and employer–employee relation

mcqs.q: Remuneration received by a Member of Parliament is taxable as:
mcqs.explain: MPs and MLAs are not Government employees, so there is no employer–employee relationship; their remuneration is income from other sources. Constituency and daily allowances have their own treatment. In practice: such income is shown under other sources in the return.
mcqs.topic: When salary is taxed (s. 15) and employer–employee relation

mcqs.q: Salary drawn by a partner from his firm is taxable as:
options: Profits and gains of business or profession
mcqs.explain: A partner is not an employee of his firm; his salary, bonus or commission from the firm is an appropriation of profit taxed as business income, as section 15 expressly provides. In practice: partners report it under business income.
mcqs.topic: When salary is taxed (s. 15) and employer–employee relation

mcqs.q: Under the default regime, house rent allowance is:
mcqs.explain: Section 202(2) denies the HRA exemption in the default regime, so the whole allowance is taxable; the Rule 279 exemption is available only to those who opt out. In practice: tenants with high rent often prefer the optional regime.
mcqs.topic: Allowances and their exemptions

mcqs.q: HRA exemption at 50% of salary applies to accommodation in:
options: Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad and Bengaluru
Only Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi and Chennai
Any city with population over 25 lakh
mcqs.explain: Rule 279 lists eight cities for the 50% limit — Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad and Bengaluru; elsewhere 40% applies. In practice: check the city of residence, not of office.
mcqs.topic: Allowances and their exemptions

mcqs.q: Children education allowance under the optional regime is exempt up to:
options: ₹3,000 per month per child, for up to two children
mcqs.explain: Children education allowance is exempt up to ₹3,000 per month per child for a maximum of two children; hostel allowance up to ₹9,000 per month per child. Both are fully taxable under the default regime. In practice: payroll restricts the exempt part automatically.
mcqs.topic: Allowances and their exemptions

mcqs.q: LTC exemption under the optional regime is available for:
options: Two journeys in a block of four calendar years
Any number of journeys in India
mcqs.explain: Rule 278 allows two journeys in a block of four calendar years (current block 2026-29), with one unavailed journey carried forward into the first year of the next block, for travel within India only. In practice: keep tickets as proof.
mcqs.topic: Allowances and their exemptions

mcqs.q: Rent-free accommodation owned by the employer in a city with population 30 lakh (2011 census) is valued at:
mcqs.explain: For employer-owned accommodation, the rate is 10% above 40 lakh population, 7.5% above 15 lakh up to 40 lakh, and 5% elsewhere, less rent paid by the employee. In practice: always use the 2011 census population of the city, not current estimates.
mcqs.topic: Valuing perquisites: accommodation and car

mcqs.q: A company car above 1.6 litres, used partly for personal purposes with all expenses met by the employer and a chauffeur provided, has a monthly perquisite value of:
mcqs.explain: The value is ₹7,000 per month for cars above 1.6 litres plus ₹3,000 for the chauffeur, i.e. ₹10,000; smaller or electric cars take ₹5,000. Only specified employees are taxed on it. In practice: logbooks support the official-use claim.
mcqs.topic: Valuing perquisites: accommodation and car

mcqs.q: Which employee is NOT a "specified employee"?
options: A non-director employee with monetary salary of ₹3.5 lakh and no shareholding
An employee with monetary salary of ₹6 lakh
mcqs.explain: Specified employees are directors, holders of 20% or more voting power, and those whose monetary salary exceeds ₹4 lakh. An employee earning ₹3.5 lakh with no such status is not specified. In practice: most managers today are specified employees.
mcqs.topic: Other perquisites and specified employees

mcqs.q: A gift voucher given by an employer is a taxable perquisite if its value is:
mcqs.explain: Gifts or vouchers below ₹15,000 are not a perquisite; at ₹15,000 or more, the whole value is taxable for all employees. In practice: festival vouchers are often kept below this limit to avoid tax for staff.
mcqs.topic: Other perquisites and specified employees

mcqs.q: An interest-free loan from an employer is a taxable perquisite where the loan exceeds:
mcqs.explain: Loans above ₹2 lakh are valued at the SBI rate on the first day of the tax year on the maximum monthly outstanding balance, less interest paid, for all employees. Smaller loans are ignored altogether. In practice: housing loans by employers often cross this limit.
mcqs.topic: Other perquisites and specified employees

mcqs.q: Employer's aggregate contribution to RPF, NPS and superannuation fund is a taxable perquisite to the extent it exceeds:
mcqs.explain: Section 17(1)(h) treats the excess over ₹7.5 lakh of combined employer contributions as a perquisite, with accretions on that excess also taxable. Employee contributions have separate interest thresholds. In practice: high earners' CTC structures watch this cap.
mcqs.topic: Provident funds, NPS and employer contributions

mcqs.q: Interest credited to a recognised provident fund is taxable to the extent it exceeds:
mcqs.explain: Interest credited to RPF above 9.5% p.a. is taxable as salary; in addition, interest on employee contributions above the ₹2.5 lakh/₹5 lakh yearly thresholds is taxable. In practice: EPF rates are currently below 9.5%, so this rarely bites ordinary employees.
mcqs.topic: Provident funds, NPS and employer contributions

mcqs.q: Deduction u/s 124(1) for employer's NPS contribution, for a private employer under the default regime, is up to:
mcqs.explain: Employer NPS contribution is deductible up to 14% of salary for Government employers, and for any employer when the employee is in the default regime; 10% for other employers under the optional regime. In practice: NPS is popular in default-regime pay structures.
mcqs.topic: Provident funds, NPS and employer contributions

mcqs.q: The maximum deduction for gratuity of a non-Government employee is:
mcqs.explain: Gratuity deductions for non-Government employees are capped at ₹20 lakh (along with actual amount and formula); Government employees deduct the whole amount. ₹25 lakh is the leave-salary cap. In practice: large gratuities above ₹20 lakh are partly taxable.
mcqs.topic: Retirement benefits: gratuity, pension, leave salary, VRS

mcqs.q: A private employee who received gratuity commutes part of pension. The deduction for commuted pension is:
options: One-third of the full commuted value of pension
One-half of the full commuted value
mcqs.explain: For non-Government employees, the deduction is one-third of the full commuted value if gratuity is also received, and one-half if not; Government employees deduct it fully. Uncommuted pension is fully taxable. In practice: compute full value = commuted amount ÷ commutation %.
mcqs.topic: Retirement benefits: gratuity, pension, leave salary, VRS

mcqs.q: Leave salary of a non-Government employee on retirement is deductible up to a maximum of:
mcqs.explain: Leave encashment on retirement is deductible to the least of ₹25 lakh, amount received, cash value of leave (30 days per year max) and ten months' average salary. Encashment during service is fully taxable. In practice: compute all four limits.
mcqs.topic: Retirement benefits: gratuity, pension, leave salary, VRS

mcqs.q: Standard deduction under the default regime is:
mcqs.explain: Section 19(1) allows standard deduction of ₹75,000 under the default regime and ₹50,000 under the optional regime, limited to salary. Professional tax is deductible only in the optional regime. In practice: pensioners also get standard deduction.
mcqs.topic: Deductions u/s 19 and computing income under both regimes

mcqs.q: Professional tax paid by a salaried employee is deductible:
options: Only if he opts out of the default regime
mcqs.explain: Section 202(2) disallows the professional tax deduction under the default regime; it is allowed under the optional regime (Table Sl. No. 1). Where the employer pays it, it is first added as a perquisite. In practice: the amount is small but should not be missed.
mcqs.topic: Deductions u/s 19 and computing income under both regimes

Employer–employee relationship essential; partners and MPs excluded.

viva.model: It is the least of the HRA received, rent paid less 10% of salary, and 50% of salary in the eight listed cities or forty percent elsewhere, and is available only under the optional regime.

kw: rent paid less|rent minus|excess of rent

viva.model: A director of the company, an employee holding twenty percent or more of the voting power, or an employee whose monetary salary exceeds four lakh rupees.

viva.q: What is the deduction for commuted pension of a private employee?
viva.model: One third of the full commuted value of pension if gratuity is also received, and one half if no gratuity is received.

viva.q: What are the limits for voluntary retirement compensation?
viva.model: Least of compensation received, five lakh rupees, three months salary for each completed year of service, and last salary multiplied by the months of service left.

viva.q: What standard deduction is allowed under each regime?
viva.model: ₹75,000 under the default regime and ₹50,000 under the optional regime, but never more than the salary itself.

cases.title: Pay package at Orbit Systems
cases.case: Priya (monetary salary ₹18 lakh) gets: a company-leased flat in Chennai (lease ₹45,000 p.m.); a 1.5-litre company car used partly for personal purposes, all expenses by the company, no chauffeur; an interest-free loan of ₹1,50,000; Diwali vouchers of ₹12,000; and the company contributes ₹8,20,000 in aggregate to her PF and NPS. She pays tax under the default regime.

mcqs.q: The flat (leased by the employer) is valued at:
options: Lower of lease rent and 10% of salary, less rent paid by her
mcqs.explain: For accommodation taken on lease by the employer, the perquisite is the lower of the lease rent and 10% of salary, minus any rent recovered. Here 10% of ₹18 lakh (₹1.8 lakh) is lower than ₹5.4 lakh lease rent. In practice: city population matters only for employer-owned houses.
mcqs.topic: Valuing perquisites: accommodation and car

mcqs.q: The company car perquisite per month is:
mcqs.explain: A car of up to 1.6 litres with expenses met by the employer and used partly for personal purposes is valued at ₹5,000 per month; ₹3,000 is added only if a chauffeur is provided. She is a specified employee. In practice: engine capacity sets the slab.
mcqs.topic: Valuing perquisites: accommodation and car

mcqs.q: The interest-free loan of ₹1,50,000 and vouchers of ₹12,000 are:
mcqs.explain: Loans up to ₹2 lakh and gifts or vouchers below ₹15,000 are not perquisites, so neither is taxed. Crossing either threshold makes them taxable perquisites. In practice: companies design benefits around these limits.
mcqs.topic: Other perquisites and specified employees

mcqs.q: Of the employer's ₹8,20,000 contribution, the amount taxable as perquisite (before any s. 124 deduction effects) is:
mcqs.explain: Employer contributions to RPF, NPS and superannuation above ₹7.5 lakh in a year are a perquisite; the excess here is ₹70,000, and income accrued on that excess is also taxable. In practice: CTC planning keeps contributions under ₹7.5 lakh.
mcqs.topic: Provident funds, NPS and employer contributions
